Toll
tōl
n. (a levy on passage or goods; rendering Aramaic halak)
From Greek telos through Old English, a tax. A toll is charged for passage — a levy on movement rather than on production.

Biblical Definition

A toll is a levy. Ezra records a Persian decree exempting the temple's servants from it: “it shall not be lawful to impose toll, tribute, or custom, upon them” — upon priests, Levites, singers, porters, Nethinims, and ministers of the house of God (Ezr 7:24). The adversaries of the rebuilding had earlier warned Artaxerxes that a restored Jerusalem would not pay “toll, tribute, and custom” (Ezr 4:13), and the work was stopped on that argument.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines toll as a tax paid for some liberty or privilege, particularly for passage over a bridge or on a highway; and a portion of grain taken by a miller for grinding.

expand to see more

TOLL, n. A tax paid for some liberty or privilege, particularly for the privilege of passing over a bridge or on a highway.

2. A liberty to buy and sell within the bounds of a manor.

3. A portion of grain taken by a miller as a compensation for grinding.

Key Scripture

Ezr 7:24 — "Also we certify you, that touching any of the priests and Levites, singers, porters, Nethinims, or ministers of this house of God, it shall not be lawful to impose toll, tribute, or custom, upon them."

Ezr 4:13 — "Be it known now unto the king, that, if this city be builded, and the walls set up again, then will they not pay toll, tribute, and custom, and so thou shalt endamage the revenue of the kings."

Ezr 4:21 — "Give ye now commandment to cause these men to cease, and that this city be not builded, until another commandment shall be given from me. Give: Chaldee, Make a decree"

Mat 17:25 — "He saith, Yes. And when he was come into the house, Jesus prevented him, saying, What thinkest thou, Simon? of whom do the kings of the earth take custom or tribute? of their own children, or of strangers?"

Modern Corruption

Religious tax exemption is defended as a right where Ezra records it as a king's gift — granted by pagan power, and therefore revocable by it.

expand to see more

Ezra 7:24 is remarkable for its source. A Persian king exempts the whole temple staff from toll, tribute, and custom — a concession that no Israelite had the power to demand. Artaxerxes grants it because he fears the wrath of the God of heaven, and the exemption exists at his pleasure. Any church that treats such privileges as inalienable rights rather than as providential gifts has forgotten how they were obtained.

Ezra 4:13 shows the other edge. Adversaries wrote to the king warning that if this city be builded… then will they not pay toll, tribute, and custom, and so thou shalt endamage the revenue of the kings — and the work stopped. The accusation that a religious community is a fiscal liability is very old, it was effective, and it is answered less by argument than by the conduct Christ prescribed when He paid the temple tax lest we should offend them.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Aramaic halak (H1983), toll or road-tax, in the Aramaic sections of Ezra; joined with middah, tribute, and belo, custom.

expand to see more

Aramaic halak (H1983) — toll, road tax; Ezra 4:13, 20, 7:24.

Aramaic middah (H4061) — tribute; the companion levy in the same verses.

Greek telos (G5056) — custom, toll; Matthew 17:25, of whom do the kings of the earth take custom or tribute?

Usage

"“It shall not be lawful to impose toll, tribute, or custom, upon them” — a pagan king's grant."

"“Then will they not pay toll… and so thou shalt endamage the revenue” — the old accusation."

"“Lest we should offend them” — Christ pays anyway."
